tasks.prompt: Create fixtures/gobench/fib/fib.go in package fib with an exported function `func Fib(n int) int` that returns the n-th Fibonacci number (Fib(0) = 0, Fib(1) = 1) using memoization, so that Fib(90) returns immediately. Only the standard library. Make sure `go build ./fixtures/gobench/fib/` succeeds. Do not run git.
gate: git diff --quiet HEAD -- fixtures/gobench/checks || { echo 'the checks were changed'; exit 1; }
go test -count=1 -timeout 30s ./fixtures/gobench/fib/ || { echo 'Fib is wrong, or too slow to be memoized (30s timeout)'; exit 1; }

tasks.prompt: Create fixtures/gobench/items/items.go in package items, using only net/http and encoding/json from the standard library, with `func NewHandler() http.Handler` serving an in-memory list of items at the path /items. An item is the JSON object {"id": <int>, "name": <string>}. GET /items returns 200 and a JSON array of all items in creation order (an empty array, not null, when there are none). POST /items with a body {"name": "..."} creates an item with the next id, starting at 1, and returns 201 with the created item as JSON; a body that is not valid JSON or has an empty name returns 400. Any other method on /items returns 405. Responses with a body set Content-Type: application/json. It must be safe for concurrent requests. Make sure `go build ./fixtures/gobench/items/` succeeds. Do not run git.
gate: git diff --quiet HEAD -- fixtures/gobench/checks || { echo 'the checks were changed'; exit 1; }
go test -count=1 -timeout 60s ./fixtures/gobench/items/ || { echo 'the handler does not meet the contract'; exit 1; }

tasks.prompt: fixtures/gobench/add/add.go has a function Add. Write a table-driven unit test for it in fixtures/gobench/add/add_test.go, covering zero, negative and positive numbers. Do not change add.go. Make sure `go test ./fixtures/gobench/add/` passes. Do not run git.
gate: git diff --quiet HEAD -- fixtures/gobench/add/add.go || { echo 'add.go was changed'; exit 1; }
test -f fixtures/gobench/add/add_test.go || { echo 'add_test.go is missing'; exit 1; }
go test -count=1 ./fixtures/gobench/add/ || { echo 'the tests fail on the correct Add'; exit 1; }

sed -i 's/return a + b/return a - b/' fixtures/gobench/add/add.go && ! go test -count=1 ./fixtures/gobench/add/ >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo 'the tests still pass when Add subtracts: they do not test it'; exit 1; }

git checkout -- fixtures/gobench/add/add.go && sed -i 's/return a + b/return a * b/' fixtures/gobench/add/add.go && ! go test -count=1 ./fixtures/gobench/add/ >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo 'the tests still pass when Add multiplies: they do not test it'; exit 1; }

tasks.prompt: Write fixtures/gobench/GOROUTINES.md: an explanation, in at most 300 words, of the difference between goroutines and operating-system threads in Go, for a developer new to Go. Cover how they are scheduled, their stack size, and their cost to create. Do not run git.
gate: test -s fixtures/gobench/GOROUTINES.md || { echo 'GOROUTINES.md is missing or empty'; exit 1; }
w=$(wc -w < fixtures/gobench/GOROUTINES.md); [ "$w" -le 300 ] || { echo "too long: $w words"; exit 1; }
grep -qi 'schedul' fixtures/gobench/GOROUTINES.md || { echo 'does not mention scheduling'; exit 1; }
grep -qi 'stack' fixtures/gobench/GOROUTINES.md || { echo 'does not mention the stack'; exit 1; }
grep -qiE 'os thread|operating.system thread|kernel thread' fixtures/gobench/GOROUTINES.md || { echo 'does not mention OS threads'; exit 1; }
